newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine labs want take patent row with US to WTO.
newsitem.headline: Argentine labs want take patent row with US to WTO.

text.p: The body grouping all major Argentine drug labs Thursday called U.S. trade sanctions "illegal" and urged President Carlos Menem to take its patent dispute with Washington to the World Trade Organization.

"(The United States) resorts to unilateral sanctions, which are illegitimate and illegal, because they have no arguments to take their claims to the WTO and back them up," the Industrial Center for Argentine Pharmaceutical Laboratories (CILFA) said.
Both Menem and the main opposition group, the Radical Party, Thursday condemned the U.S. sanctions, although Menem indicated he was willing to seek a compromise solution.
Government, opposition and local labs all said Argentina's new intellectual property rights legislation was in full compliance with all international requirements.

"It is a totally unjust sanction which has no bearing on reality, but it does not damage in the least the excellent relations between the United States and Argentina," Menem told local television. "Anyway, we will continue talking to see how we can overcome this situation."
The Radical Party called the U.S. move irksome and groundless.

Earlier in the day Menem's brother Eduardo, a senior senator, said Argentina will not toughen up its laws to please Washington. "Parliament has already fixed its position and we are going to keep it," he told local radio.

While government officials insist no laws will be changed to quell U.S. wrath, the government has yet to decree the reglamentation of a confidentiality law annex to intellectual property legislation, which could give it room to maneuver.
But the head of the lower house of Congress' Industry Committee rejected appeasement Thursday, calling instead for retaliation, according to the state-run Telam news agency.

"If we give in to the pressures ... which originate with American drug firms we would have to boost the price of drugs by up to 70 percent," said Humberto Roggero, a member of the ruling Peronist Party.

Washington said Wednesday it would withdraw half of Argentina's duty-free trade benefits as Argentine laws failed to protect U.S. drug labs. U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky said the action would affect about $260 million worth of Argentine exports to the United States.
Argentine media estimated the move would cost $10-20 million in lost exports, and officials said they did not think Washinton would be able to impose tougher sanctions.

Barshefsky said the new Argentine patent laws passed in 1995 and 1996 still allow labs to freely copy drugs developed by U.S. firms. Washington has been pressing Argentina for years to reform copyright laws, which until 1995 set no restrictions on copying foreign drug patents.
Menem, a staunch U.S. ally, has proposed legislation that would have pleased Washington, but his bills were either blocked or watered down by Congress.
